8.0.0.en: 1 Strive not with a mighty man, lest thou fall into his hands. 2 Be not at variance with a rich man, lest he lay a burden upon thee. 3 For gold hath destroyed many, and perverted the hearts of kings. 4 Strive not with a man that is full of tongue, and heap not wood upon his fire.

8.0.1.en: It is fitting for the believer to be prudent in dealing with others, so he does not quarrel with persons of authority lest they become his enemies [1]. Nor does he disturb a rich man so that he informs the ruling authorities against him (Prov 17:23). Nor does he argue with a talkative person with a loud throat who speaks much and without restraint (Prov 26:20-21).

8.0.2.en: Do not resist the mighty man sharply, lest thou fall into his hands [1].

8.0.3.en: It is not fitting for the believer to enter into a quarrel with a reckless man who brandishes a weapon, or to openly rebuke a ruler or a king and so expose himself to death in vain, unless that is a witness to the upright faith. Exempted from this are those called to martyrdom by a divine announcement, or the prophets called to confront high priests and kings, as Isaiah the prophet and John the Baptist did.

8.0.4.en: As for the believers among the people and the young priests, it is fitting for them not to destroy their energies in criticism and in trying to reform by colliding with others, but rather to light a candle instead of cursing the darkness.

8.0.5.en: It is written in the canons of Pope Peter, Seal of the Martyrs (Canon 9):

8.0.6.en: [(Those who stirred up the adversary in rashness, so as to kindle the fire of affliction, so that they enjoy martyrdom).

8.0.7.en: Those who were as though in sleep and suddenly leapt up to stir up the adversary, who was like one whose time of labor had been long, these bring upon themselves trials like the tossing of the sea and a flood of waves without number, kindling the fire (coals) of the wicked against their brethren... With these we are bound to have fellowship, because they conducted themselves so for the sake of Christ, though they did not heed His words. For He taught us to pray lest we enter into temptation, but deliver us from evil (Mt 6:13).

8.0.8.en: Perhaps they did not know that the Master of the house and our greatest Teacher often withdrew far from those who laid snares for Him, and sometimes did not walk openly because of them. And at the time of His passion He withdrew and did not deliver Himself up to them, waiting for them to come to Him with swords and staves, saying: "Are ye come out as against a thief with swords and staves for to take me?" (Mt 26:55), and they delivered Him to Pilate (Mt 27:2).

8.0.9.en: What happened with Him was repeated with His disciples who imitated Him, remembering His divine words which He spoke to strengthen us at the time of persecution, saying: "Beware of men: for they will deliver you up to the councils, and they will scourge you in their synagogues" (Mt 10:17). He says that they deliver us up, and we do not deliver ourselves up. You are brought before governors and kings for My sake, not you who present yourselves. He wants us to pass from place to place where the persecutors are, and that for the sake of His name.

8.0.10.en: Again He says: "When they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another" (Mt 10:22), as though He wants us not to thrust ourselves upon the servants of Satan and his followers, so that we may not be the cause of their double death, nor drive them to cruelty by force so that they commit deadly deeds, but He wants us to wait and be on our guard with watching and prayer, lest we enter into temptation (Mt 26:41).

8.0.11.en: Stephen (the first deacon and martyr) followed in the footsteps of the Master and endured martyrdom when the rebels seized him in Jerusalem and stoned him after bringing him before a council. He was glorified for the sake of the name of Christ, praying: "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge" (Acts 7:59).]

8.1.0.en: Do not quarrel with a rich man, lest he resist thy strength, for gold hath destroyed many, and corrupted the minds of kings [2].

8.1.1.en: Do not cling to the great and the wicked rich, lest evil cling to our nature as rust clings to iron and dust to the body.

8.2.0.en: v As rust is not the work of the smith, and dust is not placed there by the parents, so evil is not from God. Rather, God gave man a conscience and a mind so that he might avoid evil, which show him that evil is harmful and brings torments. Therefore it is fitting for you to be more careful. When you meet a man of greatness and wealth, leave the demons no room to deceive you so that you are led by him, but set death at once before your eyes, and then you will not desire anything evil or earthly [3].

8.2.1.en: St. Anthony the Great v "They that trust in their wealth, and boast themselves in the multitude of their riches." The prophet addresses this statement to two kinds of persons: to the earthborn and to the rich. He speaks to the former so that they may put away their wrong ideas of their power. And to the latter, who boast of their possessions. He says: You who trust in your strength.

8.2.2.en: These earthborn trust in the strength of the flesh, and believe that human nature is sufficient to accomplish skillfully what they wish. He says: And you who trust in the uncertainty of riches, listen. You need a ransom to be transferred to the freedom of which you were deprived when you were overcome by the power of Satan, who drew you under his dominion, for he does not leave you in freedom from his tyranny until a mighty Savior works in you, who wishes to exchange you. The ransom is not of the same kind as that which fell under his dominion, but altogether different from it, if he truly wishes to set free the captives from bondage.

8.2.3.en: Therefore the brother is unable to redeem you. No man can urge Satan to remove his dominion from him who once submitted to him! Likewise the (brother) is unable to offer to God an atonement for his own sins, so how could he have the authority to do this for others?

8.2.4.en: And what precious thing does he possess in this world that suffices to be given in exchange as the price of a soul that is precious by its nature, this soul that was created in the image of its Creator? And what work in the present time suffices to be offered to the human soul as a means and help to it in the life to come?

8.2.5.en: We may count these things as simple. For even if a man appears to have great authority in this life, even if a great number of possessions surround him, these words teach him to come down from such thinking and to humble himself under the mighty hand of God (1 Pet 5:6), not to rely on the authority of someone famous, nor to boast in the abundance of his riches. Yet he may rise a little in thought, and, with regard to those who rely on their authority or boast in their wealth, may think of the powers (and authority) of the soul, how imperfect they are in themselves to accomplish salvation. For if there were found one perfect among the sons of men, if he lacked the wisdom of God, let him not boast in anything. For even if he has gained many theories from the wisdom of the world, and gathered much of the wealth of knowledge, let him hear the whole truth of the matter: every human soul has bowed under the yoke of the bondage imposed by the common enemy of all, and being deprived of the very freedom which it received from the Creator, sin led it captive. Every captive is in need of a ransom for his freedom.

8.3.0.en: Now, a brother cannot redeem his brother, and no one can redeem himself, for he who redeems must be better than the one who was defeated and became a slave. In fact I have no man who has authority before God to make atonement for a sinner, so long as he himself is subject to sin: "For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God; being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus" our Lord (Rom 3:23-24) [4].

8.3.1.en: St. Basil the Great: Dealing with the poor and the rich: The believer who feels the burdens of the trials of his poor brethren is gentle with them in their sufferings and humiliation. When the Lord commands through Isaiah concerning the barren woman who did not bear (that is, the suffering soul), He does not use rebuke and reproof but encouragement, saying: "O thou afflicted, tossed with tempest, and not comforted, behold, I will lay thy stones with antimony, and with sapphire will I found thee..." "Fear not; for thou shalt not be ashamed; neither be thou confounded, for thou shalt not be put to shame: for thou shalt forget the shame of thy youth, and shalt not remember the reproach of thy widowhood any more. For thy Maker is thine husband; the LORD of hosts is his name" (Isa 54:11, 4).

8.4.0.en: As for the rich, let the shepherd (or the believer) instill in them the spirit of fear of pride and arrogance, for excessive gentleness with them increases their pride and makes them lose their true life. For this reason we find our Lord Jesus rebuking the rich (who trust in their riches): "Woe unto you that are rich! for ye have received your consolation" (Lk 6:24). And the Apostle Paul instructs Timothy his disciple, saying: "Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches [5], but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy..." (1 Tim 6:17). He says to him "charge," and not "hope" or "request of them." But sometimes there is a need to use David's soothing harp to drive the spirit of evil from the heart of proud Saul. Not the harp of flattery and hypocrisy, but the harp of singing in the name of the Lord, the harp of love and gentleness together with prayer, so that the Lord may give him the spirit of humility.

8.4.1.en: Nathan used the same harp with David at his fall, when he was rich. He hid the bitter medicine in his garment, using gentleness in presenting the case of the man who seized his brother's ewe lamb, and when David realized his error, Nathan was able to offer him the medicine. This is what Ben Sira suffered in the statements before us.

8.4.2.en: Do not sharply strive with the talkative man, nor heap wood upon his fire [3].

8.4.3.en: He who enters into a quarrel with a talkative person risks his reputation.

8.5.0.en: 5 Jest not with a rude man, lest thy ancestors be disgraced. 6 Reproach not a man that turneth from sin, but remember that we are all worthy of punishment.

8.5.1.en: Do not jest with an ill-bred man, lest thy ancestors be disgraced [4].

8.5.2.en: He warns us against keeping company with jesters, for jesting is unseemly, since it drives the fear of the Lord out of the heart and corrupts the talent of sanctifying time. St. Jacob of Serugh sees that God created the mouth and the tongue to train in praise and in fellowship with the heavenly beings in a life of thanksgiving. Jesting, in his view, is a deviation of the tongue from its holy work for the sake of the Kingdom of God. It is fitting for the wise man to be marked by dignity and seriousness together with gentleness, and in his kindness to be dignified and God-fearing.

8.5.3.en: Do not dishonor him who has turned away from sin in repentance, and remember that we are all worthy (of punishment on account of our sins) [5].

8.6.0.en: It is written in the Mishnah: "If a man repents, he is not told: Remember your past deeds" [6]. If someone has repented of a sin he has committed, we must not make light of him. St. Abba Moses the Black says: "Do not be hard of heart toward your brother, for we are all overcome by thoughts." But this urges us all the more toward serious repentance in the Lord.

8.7.0.en: He who understands and holds fast to godliness says: "Lord, who shall abide in thy tabernacle? who shall dwell in thy holy hill? He that walketh uprightly, and worketh righteousness, and speaketh the truth in his heart. He that backbiteth not with his tongue, nor doeth evil to his neighbour, nor taketh up a reproach against his neighbour" (Ps 15:1-3). But we reproach those who repent and those who are converted, although Holy Scripture says: Do not reproach him who has repented of sin (see Sir 8:5) [7].

8.7.1.en: v There is a man full of faith who comes toward the congregation accusing himself, disclosing to everyone the sin he has committed. Yet those who have no fear of the coming judgment of God, when they hear his words, instead of sharing his sufferings, and instead of caring for him, trouble him, and instead of falling with the fallen, they say: Get away from me and do not come near me, for I am clean! Then they begin to curse him whom they had formerly admired (when his sin was hidden), and withdraw their friendship from him.

8.8.0.en: He did not want to hide his crime. With conviction he says of those who reproach him: "My friends and my companions drew away from my plague, and my kinsmen left me" (Ps 38:11) LXX... He who, after committing a sin, desires the salvation of his soul, and does not care about the rebukes of those who do not think about their own sins and who do not remember the words of the divine Scriptures: "Do not reproach the penitent from sin, and remember that we are all worthy of punishment" (see Sir 8:5). Do not be troubled on account of these things, but be troubled on account of yourself, and pray to God to hear you and raise you after your fall, so that you may be able to say afterward: "I know my iniquity, and I grieve over my sin" (Ps 38:19) LXX [8].

8.9.0.en: 7 Dishonour not a man in his old age: for even some of us wax old. 8 Rejoice not over thy greatest enemy being dead, but remember that we die all. 9 Despise not the discourse of the wise, but acquaint thyself with their proverbs: 10 for of them thou shalt learn instruction, and how to serve great men with ease. 11 Miss not the discourse of the elders: for they also learned of their fathers, 12 and of them thou shalt learn understanding, and to give answer as need requireth.

8.9.1.en: Do not dishonor a man in his old age, for some of us also will grow old [6].

8.9.2.en: A society that makes light of the elderly makes light of its own future. It is fitting for us to benefit from the experience of those who preceded us in life, for the new generation will benefit from our experience, while acknowledging that they will be more advanced than we are. The sign of a society's vitality is continuous progress. This progress rests on what their predecessors strove for, and the new generation learns not only from the progress we have attained but also from our mistakes. Thus the generations remain in constant progress that corrects mistakes, for there will be no one perfect in everything. The present offers what is new to the future without ignoring the past.

8.9.3.en: Let us remember what the elders offered in the time of their youth, and let us not criticize them because of their bodily weakness and the weakness of their memory and their inability to practice some acts of worship, for we too may grow old one day like them. The Apostle Paul advises us: "Rebuke not an elder, but intreat him as a father; and the younger men as brethren" (1 Tim 5:1). And it is written in the book of Leviticus: "Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy God: I am the LORD" (Lev 19:32). Ben Sira calls the elders to act in a way that suits their experience and physical ability to the last breath, so that they may not fall into a feeling of despair because of idleness.

8.9.4.en: Do not rejoice over the death of a person, and remember that we shall surely all die [7].

8.9.5.en: After he has commanded us to respect the penitent sinner and the old man who is unable to work, he called us to respect the dead and his family, for he who rejoices over a dead man falls into judgment, because he does not know what was in the heart of the dead man before his death, and does not perceive God's plan for him. By death a person is joined to those who went before, so let no one rejoice over the death of his brother, for he will meet him in the life to come. Sirach sees death as a gathering with those who have gone before [7] (Gen 25:8; Judg 2:10).

8.10.0.en: v One thing is impossible for man, and that is to escape death. But if a man has fellowship with God, this is possible for man if he knows the way. If he wishes, and knows the way, he can, by faith and truth, experience the good life and be united with God [9].

8.11.0.en: v The soul that knows what the world truly is, and desires to be saved, has a strict rule, which is to think every hour within itself, saying: "It is an hour in which (death) comes, and judgment comes, when you cannot (O my soul) bear (the gaze of) the Judge, and behold, you are about to perish." By this thought the soul keeps itself from shameful pleasures [10].

8.12.0.en: What is mortal is secondary to what is immortal, and serves it, meaning that matter (the material body) serves man, and this by the compassion of God the Creator and the goodness of His being (since He granted that the body should serve the soul) [11].

8.12.1.en: St. Anthony the Great: Do not despise the words of the wise, but be diligent in their proverbs.

8.12.2.en: For from them thou shalt learn instruction, and to serve among the nobles [8].

8.12.3.en: The true believer is like the bee which gathers the nectar of various flowers and offers it as sweet and useful honey for others. Solomon the Wise says: "He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be hurt" (Prov 13:20). Ben Sira prizes the opportunities that were offered him during many journeys, where he served some of the great, yet he did not exalt himself in this work, but gathered wisdom in his thoughts and in his practices.

8.12.4.en: The story of the Lord Christ's meeting with the sinful woman in the house of Simon the Pharisee (Lk 7) reveals the existence of banquets among the notables of the Jews, where they would invite one of the teachers and hold a banquet for him, not merely to set a table for eating, but he would open the door of his house and those who wished to enjoy what was discussed with the teacher would enter.

8.13.0.en: v A man can say of those who do not wish to learn what is useful and good for them that they are not in sound health. As for those who have learned the truth and yet dispute it shamelessly, of these it is said that their sense is dead, their nature has become animal, and they do not know God, nor have their souls been enlightened by the light [12].

8.13.1.en: St. Anthony the Great: Do not ignore the saying of the elders, for they learned from their fathers, and from them thou shalt acquire understanding, and be able to answer at the proper time [9].

8.13.2.en: The ancient Jewish society esteemed the elders and their view of life through their long experience and their knowledge of the tradition handed down from the generations before them (25:4-6). Openness to learning from the elders and the wise (Lev 19:32) moves the new generation to continuous progress (Prov 22:29). For taking care to sit with the elders teaches people what they have gathered from the generations before them. It is as though sitting with a wise elder adds much to one's life, through the enjoyment of the experiences of those before, in very short periods. This is what is called tradition, where we receive from them what they received from the earlier generations, especially the living faith and the sound conduct. By this a person knows how to answer the questions that arise in his mind or that are put to him by those around him.

8.13.3.en: The ability to give the right and fitting answer is the product of listening to the tradition from the elders (Prov 22:21).

8.13.4.en: v The Lord asks of us (as believers) what He does not ask of everyone. The community of mankind lives according to the customs it receives, but the Christian's rule in life is the commandment of the Lord and the imitation of the ancient saints whose greatness of soul was manifest above every trial!

8.14.0.en: In the end it is fitting for you to leave an example for those who come after you of steadfastness (endurance) and sincere confidence in what you hope for, showing that your grief will not overcome you, but you rise above your sorrows, and are patient in sufferings, and rejoice in hope [13].

8.15.0.en: 13 Kindle not the coals of a sinner, lest thou be burnt with the flame of his fire. 14 Rise not up against a reviler, lest he lie in wait to entrap thee in thy words. 15 Lend not unto him that is mightier than thyself; for if thou lendest him, count it but lost. 16 Be not surety above thy power: for if thou be surety, take care to pay it. 17 Go not to law with a judge; for judgment is given for him according to his opinion. 18 Travel not by the way with a rash man, lest he bring trouble upon thee: for he goeth after his own will, and thou perish with him through his folly. 19 Strive not with an angry man, and go not with him into a solitary place: for blood is as nothing in his sight, and where there is no help, he will overthrow thee. 20 Consult not with a fool; for he cannot keep counsel. 21 Do not practice a secret matter before the stranger, for thou knowest not what he will bring forth. 22 Reveal not what is in thy heart to every man, lest perhaps he give thee no thanks.

8.15.1.en: Do not kindle the coals of a sinner, lest thou be burnt with the flame of his fire [10].

8.15.2.en: It is fitting for us to deal with the sinner with wisdom and love, so that we do not kindle his coals more, and so are ourselves struck by the fire of his flame. He who kindles his passions and emotions reaps extremely dangerous fruits (Prov 26:21).

8.15.3.en: Do not stand before an arrogant man, for he will provoke thee, lest he lie in wait, expecting to make thy words an ambush against thee [11].

8.15.4.en: He points to not speaking with the arrogant man, lest he provoke us to anger and we sin in our anger, and he finds an opportunity to catch the slips of our tongue.

8.15.5.en: v What need have you to cry out before the judgment? It is good to keep silence as long as the Judge is waiting; it is well not to return insult for insult, lest we too be counted among those who despise others.

8.15.6.en: Thus it is fitting for us to follow the example of that man (Job) who refuted those who attacked him by his silence. Truly he showed the strength of his spirit, since the insults did not affect him, and showed the innocence of his conscience, because he paid no heed to the accusations directed against him, but laughed at them as though they were foreign to him.

8.15.7.en: In truth, when reproaches are directed against us, and we wish to justify ourselves, we become angry and want vengeance, and by this we offer confirmation (of the accusations), for Scripture says: "Let us keep away from insult, take thy garment away, for a harmful man is passing by." And so you keep silence until he passes and does not rage and burn your garment, for it is written: "Do not kindle the coals of a sinner, lest thou be burnt with the flame of his fire" [10]. Therefore the saint keeps silent even if a servant wrongs him; and the righteous man keeps silent if a poor man reviles him; and the righteous man laughs if a sinner pours out his reproaches; and the righteous man blesses if a weak person curses him.

8.16.0.en: David kept silence when Shimei the son of Gera cursed him (2 Kgs 16:5-14). And Job laughed (Job 19:7) LXX, and Paul blessed, saying: "Being reviled, we bless" (1 Cor 4:12) [14].

8.16.1.en: St. Ambrose: Suretyship and the responsibility of the sponsor: Do not lend to one who is stronger than thou, and if thou lendest him anything, count it as lost [12].

8.16.2.en: It is good to support our brethren by giving generously, and at the same time with wisdom, lest we give an opportunity to one who is not in need to borrow from us and not repay the loan. By this we would have sinned against him, since we open for him the door of greed and exploitation of others, and against ourselves, since we are counted unfaithful in what God has given us.

8.16.3.en: Do not be surety above thy power, and if thou be surety, take care as one who is bound to pay [13].

8.16.4.en: Suretyship was a common custom in Israel, and the proverbs warned against practicing it carelessly or beyond our ability. Though the believer is bound to love everyone, the practice of love requires prudence and conduct with wisdom. Here he warns us of two matters concerning suretyship:

8.16.5.en: First: a man should not lend to one who is stronger than he [12], that is, one who is on a higher social level than he. Truly God requires us to give to widows and orphans and those who are in distress out of need, but he who gives to one who is not in need and who is a man of authority, as a kind of display of wealth, expecting that the debt may not be returned to him, is unfaithful in the management of the money the Lord has given him, while the needy were more deserving of this money.

8.16.6.en: Second: let no one stand surety for anyone for what he is not able, as surety, to return to the creditor.

8.16.7.en: v Beloved dear ones, consider those who offer themselves as sureties for someone with regard to money (or a loan), how they expose themselves to great danger... Indeed, if the person who received the loan has shown himself good, he returns what he borrowed to the one who guaranteed him. But if he turns into a wicked person, he causes disaster to the one who stood surety. Therefore the Wise Man warns us: "If thou be surety, take care to pay it" (see Sir 8:13).

8.16.8.en: If this is the case with the surety concerned with money, who is bound to be responsible for everything, how much more those who stand surety in spiritual matters and in the matter of virtue, since he is bound to show great vigilance and watchfulness, by urging and showing fatherly tenderness. It is fitting for (the sponsors) not to take the matter lightly, for you are in danger.

8.17.0.en: The benefit will be shared if they offer personal counsel to lead the person in the way of virtue, while their judgment will be grave if they neglect this. For this reason it has become customary to call these (sponsors) spiritual fathers [15].

8.17.1.en: St. John Chrysostom: Do not go to law with a judge, for judgment is given for him because of his position [14].

8.17.2.en: This does not mean laxity in claiming our rights even from men of the judiciary, but we must use the lawful channels with deliberation and prudence. It is fitting for the believer to realize that it is impossible to win a case he brings against a judge.

8.17.3.en: Do not travel on a journey with a rash man, lest by his weight he bring thee down.

8.17.4.en: For he goeth after his own will, and thou perish with him through his folly [15].

8.17.5.en: One must not accompany a rash man on his journeys, lest he push us into venturing without consideration, which causes us troubles.

8.18.0.en: Do not fight with the angry man, nor go with him into the wilderness, for to him the shedding of blood is as nothing, and where there is no helper for thee, there he will overthrow thee [16].

8.18.1.en: Let us beware of the man filled with hatred and fury, for he is driven even to shed blood. Rather, it is fitting for us to stand far from the man who gives himself over to anger.

8.19.0.en: Do not consult with a fool, for he cannot keep the secret [17].

8.19.1.en: It is fitting for us not to share our thoughts with those who are not worthy of trust [17-19]. Otherwise, in the wrong of simplicity, we ask counsel of a foolish person who does not keep the secret. Nor is it permissible to disclose our secrets to everyone, and therefore the Church asks that a person be frank with his father of confession, who has no right to divulge the secrets of the penitent to anyone, whatever his worldly or ecclesiastical position, neither openly nor by hint.

8.20.0.en: Do not practice a secret matter before a stranger, for thou knowest not what he will bring forth [18].

8.20.1.en: It is wise not to utter secret matters before a stranger whom we do not know to what extent he keeps a secret.

8.20.2.en: Do not reveal thy heart to every man, lest he show thee no harshness [16] [19].

8.20.3.en: It is wise not to disclose what is in our heart to a man whose nature we do not know, for he may turn into a fierce enemy.

8.21.s.en: Let me deal with everyone in Your presence!

8.21.0.en: v My God, my Savior and my Leader, beloved of my soul, I need Your divine presence that I may walk in the spirit of wisdom.

8.21.1.en: Sanctify my mind, my heart, my mouth, and my whole being, that I may know how to deal with each person in love together with wisdom, with kindness and tenderness without laxity, so that no one perishes, but all see You manifested in all my conduct.

8.21.2.en: v I do not fear a mighty man who has authority, but without partiality I love him, and seek the salvation of his soul.

8.21.3.en: And with wisdom I do not enter into strife with him, lest I waste my time and destroy the purity of my heart and mind.

8.21.4.en: Let him see You as the secret of my strength and my authority!

8.21.5.en: Rather, I crush the devil under my feet in a spirit of courage together with humility.

8.21.6.en: Let him see me hidden in You, so that he dares not come near me.

8.21.7.en: v In a spirit of tenderness I draw near to the rich man, not desiring anything of what he has, for You are my riches and my eternal wealth.

8.21.8.en: Let the rich man touch my inner peace and my constant joy, and feel his need of You, O Giver of the riches of spirit, soul, and body!

8.21.9.en: Let him realize the passing away of the first heaven and earth, and look forward to enjoying the new heaven and the new earth.

8.21.10.en: Let the whole world become small in his eyes, and let him ask You for the speed of Your coming that he may be enriched by Your heavenly glories.

8.21.11.en: v I look upon the talkative man, and I ask You to set a guard over my mouth and a strong door over my lips.

8.21.12.en: Who is the guard but Your Holy Spirit, who will not allow a vain, useless word to come out of my mouth.

8.21.13.en: And who is it that sanctifies my lips and teaches me when to be silent and when to speak, and what to utter.

8.21.14.en: v Let the words of unrestrained jesting pass by, so that I do not find them pleasant, but find sweet Your commandment which gives me comfort and joy.

8.21.15.en: v Remove from my mind the sins of the repentant man, so that I do not remember his weaknesses, but see him clothed in the garments of Your righteousness, O my God.

8.21.16.en: Let me see him go before many, hastening toward eternal glory.

8.21.17.en: I do not make light of his repentance, but seek the salvation of my own soul and the salvation of all my brethren.

8.21.18.en: v If I see an old man unable to stand for prayer, or to practice fasting and prostrations, let me remember that old age is not far from me, and sickness may strike me in moments.

8.21.19.en: I realize my weakness and pray for the old and the sick, asking growth for all the sons of men.

8.21.20.en: v If I take part in the prayer for one of the departed, I long for the hour of my departure from the world to arrive.

8.21.21.en: I do not recall his sins, but I count him blessed because he is going to You, sharing with the heavenly beings and with our beloved departed in a wonderful heavenly choir.

8.21.22.en: v As for the wise and the self-sacrificing servants, I count meeting them a gift from You.

8.21.23.en: I count myself a little bee that gathers nectar from every flower, offering it as sweet and useful honey to many, with no merit of mine in it.

8.21.24.en: v If I meet a furious man, I do not criticize him, lest his anger be kindled all the more and I be burned with him by the fire of his flame.

8.21.25.en: And if I meet an arrogant man, I remember my former weaknesses, and keep silence while praying fervently for him.

8.21.26.en: v I do not lend to a man who is not in need and who is stronger than I.

8.21.27.en: For what You have given me is a trust for the needy and poor.

8.21.28.en: v Take hold of my hands and lead me, that I may walk in You, and complete all the days of my sojourn in joy and peace.
